Ophthalmology · published research

Ocular hypertension

Human reports describe a transient intraocular-pressure reduction after a single light exposure, but durable pressure control has not been shown. Retinal ganglion-cell protection is limited to animal work.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Human reports describe a transient intraocular-pressure reduction after a single light exposure, but durable pressure control has not been shown. Retinal ganglion-cell protection is limited to animal work.

Summary of the Evidence

Three publications appear in the exact ocular-hypertension category: two human reports and one rat study. The human evidence comprises a small controlled single-session comparison and a case series proposing an irradiation response as a diagnostic test. They address acute pressure change, not sustained treatment. Ivandic et al. 2009 Dimitrova et al. 2019

Human and clinical evidence

The 2009 case series included 123 patients and 211 eyes and studied a low-intensity irradiation test to distinguish normotensive from hypertensive responses. It reported short-term pressure decreases in some eyes, but this was not a longitudinal treatment trial. A 2019 controlled study involving 34 participants measured pressure before and after one infrared exposure; the irradiation group declined from a mean of 16.67 to 15.27 mmHg, while the control group changed from 15.71 to 15.21 mmHg. The small study and short interval do not establish lasting pressure control or clinical benefit.

Animal evidence

One rat report found that red light attenuated retinal ganglion-cell death in a raised-intraocular-pressure model. This outcome concerns retinal injury, not sustained pressure lowering in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The mapped animal publication also includes culture work addressing cell death. No separate human ex-vivo study is listed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinical reports used low-intensity infrared or laser irradiation in single-session protocols, while the rat study used focused red light. The target tissue, wavelength, exposure geometry, and outcome differ. No repeat-treatment schedule or clinically validated dose for chronic ocular hypertension is established.

Interpretation

The evidence supports only an acute physiological response in some settings. A single measurement change is not equivalent to durable pressure control or glaucoma prevention. Longitudinal controlled studies with masked pressure measurement and optic-nerve outcomes are absent.

Evidence strength in source summaryAcute intraocular-pressure response: Limited signal Durable pressure control: Not demonstrated Retinal ganglion-cell protection: Preclinical only
Publications and records3 publications: 2 human reports, including 1 controlled single-session study and 1 diagnostic case series, plus 1 rat publication with culture work.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small human reports describe short-term pressure changes after irradiation, including one single-session diagnostic response rather than sustained treatment. A rat study examines retinal ganglion-cell injury after raised pressure. No study demonstrates durable pressure lowering or prevention of glaucoma progression.

Publication and study types

  • The case series reports 123 patients and 211 eyes; the controlled study reports 34 participants.
  • Cohort overlap is not indicated, but neither report demonstrates durable treatment benefit.
